title: Do You Have Any Pet Peeves About Reading
author: Timothy Shanahan
summary: Timothy Shanahan, a foundational reading researcher, presents 10 pet peeves about reading education, reposted from 2021 with minor updates. The peeves range from the incoherence of 'balanced literacy' as a concept (no one agrees on what is being balanced or what balance means) to the Reading Wars' 'end the wars' rhetoric (which Shanahan reads as a demand that the pro-phonics side stand down). He criticizes educators who seek research to support decisions they have already made, teachers who love one aspect of literacy and teach it at the expense of others, and phonics advocates who invoke the 'science of reading' label while sneaking in practices without evidence. Two peeves with direct classroom implications: brief one-on-one conferences do not produce the deep thinking that 20-30 minute group discussions do, and 'instructional level' text placement has been set too easy for decades, protecting students from the productive challenge they need.
points: Balanced literacy is not a coherent program but a 'shell game' -- no agreed components, no agreed definition of balance -- functioning as a socially reassuring term that camouflages chronically under-resourced skills instruction, particularly phonics and fluency.

The 'end the Reading Wars' call typically means one side (pro-phonics, research-backed) should stand down so the other can continue ignoring an impressive body of evidence; Shanahan argues for less war-anxiety and more specification of what a comprehensive, research-based program actually includes.

Brief one-on-one student conferences do not produce deep thinking -- only group discussion of 20-30 minutes, with diverse reader reactions and sustained probing, achieves the interpretive depth that literary understanding requires.

Research on 'instructional level' text placement shows leveled books have been set too easy for decades -- protecting students from productive struggle while preventing them from reaching the highest achievement levels they could attain with adequate support.

Science-of-reading advocates who champion phonics research but then 'sneak in' unvalidated practices (sound walls, decodable-text-only, extra-heavy phonemic awareness programs) create a credibility problem that undermines evidence-based reform.
quotes: It should be obvious that 'balanced literacy' isn't really a thing. It's a shell game. No one agrees on the essential components or even on what balance means, it's just another feel-good term, socially appealing, but without any real meaning.

Those who profess to want to end the reading wars seem to think the best way to do that is for the pro-phonics people to stand down, so that the anti-phonics people can continue to ignore the impressive body of research supporting its teaching.

There is no research supporting this weird idea. I can't understand why anyone would believe it. My hunch is that those who make the claim have never, themselves, participated in any kind of rich, rigorous discussions of literature or 'great books.'
Teachers tend to devote more time to what they're comfortable with, and less to what they know less or care about less. Instead of avoiding what you don't like, bone up on the areas you don't know.

I'm happy that parents, school boards, and state legislatures are championing the science of reading. Page 1 Article Archive -- Education & Leadership Unfortunately, not everyone who promotes that idea is especially serious about it. They insist on following the science when it comes to phonics, but then sneak in stuff like sound walls, decodable texts, extra heavy doses of phonemic awareness instruction, and whole book teaching with no science in sight.
The history of science often reveals that what's 'obvious' or 'logical' just isn't true. That's the benefit of a science of reading. It depends on evidence, not claims." Page 2
